extracted.intended_audience: nobles, courtiers, and those training or evaluating courtly behavior (readers of Renaissance courtly conduct)
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the personal, physical, martial, and social qualities that constitute the ideal Renaissance courtier and guidance (examples and anti‑patterns) for exhibiting them in court life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility of birth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should be nobly born and of gentle race; noble birth is like a bright lamp that manifests and makes visible good and evil deeds and kindles and stimulates to virtue by fear of shame and hope of praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: noble birth brings social expectations, easier first impressions, and a stimulus to preserve family honour. Counterargument acknowledged (humble birth can produce virtue), but for the purpose of describing a Courtier 'without flaw' the speaker insists on nobility to secure universal opinion and immediate esteem. Examples: nobles achieve instant reputation whereas low-born must exert effort and time to create the same impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural endowments: talent, beauty, and 'air' (grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should be endowed by nature not only with talent and beauty of person and feature, but with a certain grace and (as we say) air that shall make him at first sight pleasing and agreeable to all who see him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ornament should dispose and unite all his actions and promise his worth. Some people are born richly endowed and need little training; others can be improved by study and toil. Example: the Cardinal Don Ippolito d'Este is cited as embodying such innate grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as universal seasoning of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier must accompany his actions, gestures, habits — in short his every movement — with grace; grace is treated as an almost universal seasoning without which other qualities are of little worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace may be natural or (to an extent) acquired by pains and training. Anti‑patterns: affectations (curling hair, plucking brows, glossing face) that make a man effeminate and limp mannerisms. The speaker notes the practical difficulty of teaching grace and distinguishes between those naturally graceful and those who can cultivate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary profession: proficiency in arms
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal and true profession of the Courtier ought to be that of arms; he should follow it actively above all else, be known as bold and strong, and be loyal to whomsoever he serves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martial skill must be practised constantly; reputation for martial courage is essential and once tarnished (by cowardice) remains infamous. The Courtier need not be a full commander but must show perfect loyalty and unconquered courage. Examples: valour recognized in small occurrences as well as great ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage genuine, not performative
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should show ardour and courage even when not expected to be observed; true courage is present in little as well as great matters and is not merely for show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with men who perform bravado only before spectators and act cowardly in private. The ideal is internal strength of mind visible in all circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation and impudent self‑praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should avoid ostentation and that impudent self‑praise by which men excite hatred and disgust; self‑praise must be discreet and appear natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted is modest or artful self‑commendation when deserved: 'the art consists in saying things in such a way that they shall not seem to be said to that end.' Anti‑patterns: indiscriminate boasting, blustering, or pretension; anecdotal examples (man who refused dance saying 'to fight' etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate physical build and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier's bodily frame should be neither extremely short nor tall; rather well built and shapely of limb, showing strength, lightness, and suppleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremes of height invite contempt; very large men are often dull and unfit for agile exercises. Prefer slight shortness to excessive tallness. The body should support agility and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill with weapons on foot and on horseback
rubrics_metrics.description: He should handle every sort of weapon well on foot and on horse, understand the advantages of each, and be familiar with the weapons ordinarily used among gentlemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicality: duels or disputes may require using whatever weapon is at hand, so general familiarity is 'a very safe thing.' This is valued both for war and for gentlemanly differences that become duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrestling and close‑combat competence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very important to know how to wrestle, for it is a great help in the use of all kinds of weapons on foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrestling enhances effectiveness in close quarters and complements weapons training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement, prudence, and readiness in quarrels/duels
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier must understand the quarrels and differences that may arise, be quick to seize an advantage, and always show courage and prudence; he should not be too ready to fight except when honour demands it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compelled to fight he must be most deliberate both in preliminaries and in the duel itself, showing readiness and daring. Avoid rashness; measure risk and act deliberately when honour obliges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defensive‑only or cowardly tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should not fritter an affair away by selecting weapons that neither cut nor pierce, arm as if expecting a cannonade, or stand ever on the defensive and retreat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behaviour merits the severest censure and makes one a laughingstock; anti‑pattern exemplified by recent foolish duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior horsemanship and excellence in national arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should be a perfect horseman in every kind of seat, understand horses and riding, and excel in the particular exercises prized among nations (e.g., Italians: riding with the rein, tilting; French: arts of defence and attack; Spaniards: casting spears and darts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He should temper all movements with good judgment and grace. Strive to be eminent in the nation's specialty while maintaining universal grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manly exercises beyond arms: hunting, athletics, and games
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises closely connected with arms — hunting (the chase), swimming, leaping, running, throwing stones, tennis, vaulting on horse — greatly foster manly sturdiness and show disposition of the body, quickness and suppleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tennis demonstrates quickness and suppleness; vaulting makes a man light and dexterous and, when accompanied by grace, is a finer show than many others. These exercises also win public esteem, which matters at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mountebank stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should leave to others feats like turning somersaults, rope‑walking, and similar tricks which savour of the mountebank and little befit a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between respectable athletic/martial skills and lowly entertainments; avoid degrading oneself with circus‑style spectacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify life with social arts while preserving discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should sometimes descend to quieter and more tranquil exercises — laugh, jest, banter, frolic and dance — yet always appear genial and discreet and never depart from praiseworthy deeds or good judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social activities should be governed by grace so that everything he does or says is stamped with it; this helps avoid envy and entertains all ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a strong favourable first impression
rubrics_metrics.description: He ought to strive to make a good one at the outset, since first impressions are powerful: when one Courtier is known to be a gentleman and another is not, the noble is instantly more esteemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First impressions persist and guide judgments; social favour and initial reputation can create long‑lasting esteem even if the person's true worth is later revealed. Thus initial comportment and appearance matter greatly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate virtue and grace through study and toil
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a middle state between perfect grace and senseless folly; those not perfectly endowed by nature can, with study and toil, in great part polish and amend their natural defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouragement that natural deficit is not absolute: with proper training many qualities (especially manners and some grace) can be improved, even if the speaker claims he cannot personally teach all the practical skills.
